text: This is an illustrative scenario, not a report on a real company. Lesson 30's game day ended with a question nobody could answer with confidence: was anything else silently depending on the region that had just gone down? The honest answer turned out to be yes, and finding it took a second look at infrastructure nobody had put on the original dependency map at all.

On paper, Wrenhaven's checkout path was genuinely redundant. Compute ran in both regions. The database had a real, working auto-failover group. Redis was geo-replicated. Front Door routed globally to whichever region was healthy. None of this was theatrical -- it was real engineering, done correctly, at the layer most dependency checks stop at, and Lesson 29's scoped test had already passed against exactly this architecture.

During the full-outage rehearsal, failover ran exactly as planned, and checkout-api in Central US came up and immediately failed every request. It wasn't missing a database or a route -- it was missing the credentials to use either one, because every service in both regions pulled its secrets from one Key Vault instance that lived only in the region the drill had just declared unreachable.

Chapter 4's dependency map had recorded checkout-api depends on Key Vault as a single edge, true but incomplete. It never asked which region that dependency actually ran in, or whether the secondary's survival quietly depended on the primary's. The same blind spot hides just as easily behind a shared DNS provider or a single identity tenant both regions call to authenticate -- the pattern is identical.

The fix deploys a second vault in Central US, replicates secrets into it on a real monitored schedule, and points each region at its own vault first with a tested fallback order -- never one hardcoded reference anywhere in the fleet. But the actual lesson is step four: re-running the dependency-mapping exercise against every existing edge, asking whether the thing on the other end is itself region-redundant, or just assumed to be.

Application-layer redundancy means nothing if every redundant copy still shares one invisible, unredundant dependency underneath it. The next hidden single point of failure won't announce itself -- it will look exactly like a dependency nobody thought to question twice. Lesson 32 closes this chapter, this course, and the entire fifteen-course path that led here.
